_comment: Every statement this project makes about itself, with the state the recorded
measurements are expected to be in. `verify` checks this file against results/.
expect: 'holds'  - the statement is true and must stay true.
'fails'  - a known, accepted limitation. It is written down so that it
cannot be quietly forgotten, and so that fixing it is a
deliberate act that updates this file.
'not_exercised' - the profile cannot reach the condition.
A finding that flips in EITHER direction fails verification. A claim that
expected a real result but got 'not_exercised' also fails: an untested hazard
must never read as a green build.

findings.because: Append latency is long-tailed: inline merge_key holds both the shard lock and the appender lock while it decompresses, concatenates, recompresses and rewrites a key's whole run. The design document reports only throughput means, which cannot show this.
No single append should stall for more than 50ms. This currently holds at ci profile and is the guard that would catch inline merging getting worse.

Write throughput does not scale with writer threads. seal_shard takes the single appender mutex inside its per-extent loop and flush_builder takes it twice consecutively, so the write path convoys. Measured at 19% efficiency and negative absolute scaling at 4 threads. Every db_bench comparison in the design document is single-threaded, which is the configuration that hides this.

Open is no longer proportional to key count but is not independent of it either: 0.0ms at 100k keys against 0.6ms at 10M, so 100x the keys cost 20x the open. What remains is the block table, which is still decoded per entry. The key index, which used to dominate this, no longer contributes. Pinned to full: at ci scale the key counts are too small for an open to resolve at all -- F2.1 holds there and fails here, which is a property of the clock rather than of the engine. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

FIXED by the mapped key index. Open grew 196x for 100x the keys while the reader decoded the index into Vec<(Vec<u8>, Extents)> and hashed it; it now grows 20x, because opening validates a header and stops. At 10M keys that is 0.6ms against 2406ms. F2.1 still fails -- 20x is sub-linear, not independent -- since the index is still read from a file whose size grows with the key count. Pinned to full: at ci scale the key counts are too small for an open to resolve at all -- F2.1 holds there and fails here, which is a property of the clock rather than of the engine. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.
A 1,000-op durability window costs 25x throughput, because checkpoint() rewrites the whole key index rather than what changed.

FIXED by turning block compression off. A 20,000-op window sustains 199,308 ops/s with about 2MB at risk -- the first usable point this curve has had. checkpoint() still rewrites the whole key index, so the floor grows with key count rather than with what changed, and F4.1 still fails at 38x; what changed is that the write path is now fast enough that the floor sits somewhere usable. Measured at ci, which is not citable for the throughput figure itself -- the claim is that a point exists, and its existence is not a ci artifact.
Every reader process must see a complete, self-consistent checkpoint state. This is the core safety property of the append-only design and must never regress.

WITHDRAWN as an ordering. `supdb` does not commit durably and LMDB does, and `supdb` checksums and LMDB does not; both axes could have been equalized and neither was. The suite recorded 863,005 ops/s against 674,858 and called it a 1.28x win for as long as this claim has existed, with the difference sitting in a features table two lines away. It was never a load result. EXT.9 and EXT.10 are the comparisons, at both levels of promise: matched durable, Supdb loses 91x; matched non-durable, it loses 1.85x. `Features::unmatched` now refuses to rank a pair that differs on an equalizable axis, so this cannot recur by being forgotten.

WITHDRAWN as an ordering: `supdb` verifies checksums and LMDB has none to verify. This one ran in the direction nobody was watching -- the unmatched figure is 994,780 reads/s against LMDB's 1,093,321, so Supdb was *behind* here while paying a cost its comparator does not. f8 prices verification at +8.5% on writes. Equalized, EXT.11 reads 1.042x at p=0.2013, which is parity. The point of matching is not that it flatters Supdb; it is that unmatched comparisons are not comparisons whichever way they fall.

WITHDRAWN as an ordering, same reason as EXT.4: the checksum axis was never equalized and a scan verifies. Recorded unmatched at 27,798,545 entries/s against LMDB's 39,940,773. EXT.12 is the matched version and reads 0.785x, so equalizing recovers some of the gap and does not close it. The prose here used to say '0.65x' and point at the ext-sweep decomposition as the stable thing to read instead; both halves were wrong, and the decomposition turned out to be a straight line fitted through a bent curve. See EXT.7 and EXT.8.

BROKEN by the same change, and deliberately. Supdb stores 4.7MB against LMDB's 2.6MB where it used to be smaller. Uncompressed data plus an uncompressed mapped index cost the space axis outright. That was one of only two axes Supdb led on, and it was traded knowingly for 3.6x on reads, 30x on scans and 3.8x on writes -- see f12. Turning Options::compress back on restores it.

FIXED by `Store::read_all`. YCSB-A (50/50 read/write) now runs 1,750,629 ops/s against read-only YCSB-C's 2,304,688 -- 0.76x, where it was 13.5x slower. A read no longer needs a checkpoint and a fresh Reader; the writer reads its own sealed, staged and pending state directly, and a sealed extent is served from a mapping rather than by preading its whole 64KiB block. Against LMDB the mixed workloads went from 0.07-0.14x to 20.98x on A and 18.40x on F. This was the last structural thing between Supdb and the workload shape no benchmark in the design document contains.

A cold measurement must be able to prove it was cold. The design document confesses that its earlier cold-read numbers were served from pages the JVM had pinned across drop_caches, invalidating all of them.
The ci profile builds 64MB on a 16GB machine, so the dataset never leaves the page cache. Recorded as not-exercised rather than passing, because an untested hazard must not read as a green build.

Measured at 23.0GB against 15.7GB of RAM: 338,681 reads/s resident against 370 out-of-core, a 916x degradation. The engine reads through a read-only mmap with no madvise anywhere, so it has no readahead control, no asynchronous I/O and no influence over eviction -- the failure modes Crotty et al. (CIDR'22) enumerate. MECHANISM FOUND: f23-madvise reproduces this collapse under a memory cgroup and attributes it to readahead thrashing -- 86,977x read amplification with the default advice against 141x with MADV_RANDOM, and 25.2x on throughput. The engine still has no asynchronous I/O and no influence over eviction, so this remains a failing claim, but 'no madvise anywhere' is now a measured cause rather than a plausible one.
Out-of-core read latency is bimodal: p50 0.155ms but p99 9.5ms and max 81ms. Every cache miss is a synchronous page fault the engine cannot see coming or overlap.
The precondition: the stored file must exceed the memory available to cache it. 23.0GB against 15.7GB, ratio 1.47.

Index size still grows with key count -- 13.5MB at 250k keys, 866MB at 16M -- which no layout change fixes: an index of N keys holds N records. What changed is the constant, 57 B/key against 131, and that the bytes are shared between readers instead of duplicated.

Reader open grows with key count, though no longer in proportion to it, and what remains is the block table rather than the key index. The index is 89 bytes per key in a mapped section readers share -- it was 131 heap-resident and duplicated per process, then 57, then 74.8 in the previous full record -- and the number decomposes exactly on this shape: 16.8 B of hash slots (a power of two at twice the keys), 12 B of directory (8 B a key plus the half-again room `index_inserts` reserves; 4 B before that became the default), and 60 B of records, a 16-byte key's 40-byte record under the flat index's half-again slack, of which format v5's count field is the 4 B that took a record from 36 to 40. So v5 costs 6 B a key here, 7%, and `index_inserts` 8; both are recorded rather than netted.

At 57 B/key one reader fills this machine's 15.7GB at 297M keys and eight readers reach it at 37.1M keys each, against 16.1M each before the index was made shareable. The headroom is understated, since the eight now share one file-backed copy rather than holding eight.

FIXED. get_uvarint no longer reads past the end of its buffer or shifts without bound; emit, scan and the index decoder validate every length against the bytes actually remaining; and extent block ids are validated once at index-build time rather than at each of the four read paths that index self.blocks with them. 0 panics in 3,317 damage trials.

FIXED by adding checksums: CRC-32C per chunk in the chunk directory, so a point read verifies only what it decodes, plus a whole-block CRC in the block index for blocks stored verbatim or compressed as a single stream. The statement was also corrected twice: it previously measured how much damage went unnoticed, which at 73% was mostly size-class padding, and then at 7.5% was mostly chunks orphaned inside live blocks. The engine's actual obligation is that a read returns written bytes or an error, and that now holds at 0/3,317.

FIXED. delete() and put() now drop matching entries from Shard::members, so an extent staged in the block builder by an inline seal cannot be pushed back onto a key that was deleted or replaced. Reproducer in tests/known_bugs.rs, no longer ignored.
A store killed after at least one checkpoint must open. It does, across every trial -- the alternating superblock slots work. This is a genuine strength of the design.
Recovery must invent nothing: every value read back after a crash was actually written.
Recovery must lose only a suffix. About 95% of keys survive a mid-run crash.

A store killed before its first checkpoint does not open at all -- there is no superblock to find. Everything written lives in per-shard memory buffers and buffer_bytes defaults to 512MB, so the window in which a crash loses everything is not small.

The next engine opens after a crash at any point. 120/120 directories opened at full: 82 crashes had a seal in flight, 72 a merge, 72 landed with partitions, 41 tore the header of a freshly rotated WAL. The manifest is the swap point, the orphan sweep removes what it does not name, and replay stops at the last intact commit frame. The header case needed a fix before it held: replay refused a WAL shorter than its magic, and a rotated WAL's header is unsynced until its first commit; a prefix of the magic is now an empty WAL and open rewrites it (crash-plan.md P4.1).

Under Sync::Always every acknowledged commit survives: 60/60 crashes reopened at or past the last acknowledged batch, with the live WAL's unsynced tail torn to a random length first. This is the statement EXT.22's durable load rests on. The self-check is `--tear-synced`: let the tear reach below the synced mark and 3/4 trials lose an acknowledged batch, so the parent can see one (P4.2).

What survives is an exact prefix of the commit order: the parent regenerates the child's stream from its seed and every one of 120 recovered states, deletes and transactions included, equalled the state after some whole number of batches; count agreed with read_all on every key and scan with both (P4.3).
Recovery invents nothing: every value read back across 120 crashes was byte for byte the one its sequence number wrote (P4.4).

Under Sync::EveryN(8) a crash loses at most seven acknowledged batches and only from the tail: 60/60 within the bound, the most lost 6, with up to 48,248 bytes torn from the unsynced tail. A process kill alone could not have tested this -- the page cache outlives the process -- which is why the parent tears the tail itself (P4.5).
Supdb reads 2.878x faster than redb (p=0.0022) over seven interleaved repetitions. LMDB is behind Supdb here too (EXT.4), so this is first place rather than second.

FIXED, by two changes. Appender::release now refuses an unbalanced release instead of absorbing it -- the old saturating guard did not prevent a double free, it guaranteed one, pushing the same slot into the free list twice. And seal_shard now clears entry.extents in the same breath as releasing the superseded blocks, so the index can never name a block whose refcount has already reached zero.

Block checksums must cost less than 10% of write throughput. Measured interleaved in one process, not by subtracting two runs -- when that was tried the unchanged comparators in the external suite moved +20% to +43% between runs, so the apparent effect was mostly machine drift.
Same for read throughput. Hardware CRC-32C on x86-64 with a portable slice-by-8 fallback; a byte-at-a-time IEEE table cost 13-35% of writes and was replaced.
Four bytes per chunk plus one per block. Space is the axis this design wins on, so the cost is bounded explicitly. Unlike the timing figures this one is immune to machine drift.

An mmap-able layout at least 1.5x smaller than the current index must exist, or the whole argument for replacing it collapses. hash+flat is 1.8x smaller and mph+paged 4.5x. Pinned to full: these thresholds are calibrated at 10M keys, and at ci scale (100k) every structure fits in cache and the ordering differs. Pinned to x86_64: the thresholds are calibrated for 64-byte cache lines and 4 KiB pages, and Apple Silicon has 128-byte lines and 16 KiB pages.

hash+flat looks up within 1.5x of the current heap hash (1.29x at 10M, p=0.0022). The index is about a fifth of a point read, so that is roughly +5% end to end -- the price of an O(1) open and cross-process sharing. Pinned to full: these thresholds are calibrated at 10M keys, and at ci scale (100k) every structure fits in cache and the ordering differs. Pinned to x86_64: the thresholds are calibrated for 64-byte cache lines and 4 KiB pages, and Apple Silicon has 128-byte lines and 16 KiB pages.

A bulk-loaded B+tree is not on the frontier: a plain packed array is both faster and smaller. Loaded here at 100% fill, which flatters it. This is the measured answer to whether copying LMDB's index is worth doing. Pinned to full: these thresholds are calibrated at 10M keys, and at ci scale (100k) every structure fits in cache and the ordering differs. Pinned to x86_64: the thresholds are calibrated for 64-byte cache lines and 4 KiB pages, and Apple Silicon has 128-byte lines and 16 KiB pages.

No composite scans as fast as the current heap layout, whose entries are one contiguous Vec. Its advantage is partly allocation locality in a freshly built index and would be expected to erode in a long-lived process, which is not measured. Pinned to full: these thresholds are calibrated at 10M keys, and at ci scale (100k) every structure fits in cache and the ordering differs. Pinned to x86_64: the thresholds are calibrated for 64-byte cache lines and 4 KiB pages, and Apple Silicon has 128-byte lines and 16 KiB pages.

A blocked Bloom filter at least halves absent-key lookups (667 -> 239 ns) for about 2.7 B/key. This is the one dedicated structure that wins a category outright, and it exists specifically because a minimal perfect hash has no cheap way to fail. Pinned to full: these thresholds are calibrated at 10M keys, and at ci scale (100k) every structure fits in cache and the ordering differs. Pinned to x86_64: the thresholds are calibrated for 64-byte cache lines and 4 KiB pages, and Apple Silicon has 128-byte lines and 16 KiB pages.

A minimal perfect hash reaches 22.2 B/key -- 4.5x smaller than today -- but at 801 ns against 369, so it does not deliver hash-class speed. BBHash probes several level bit-arrays plus a rank index, which is more cache misses than one hash probe rather than fewer. It is another point on the frontier, not a way past it. Pinned to full: these thresholds are calibrated at 10M keys, and at ci scale (100k) every structure fits in cache and the ordering differs. Pinned to x86_64: the thresholds are calibrated for 64-byte cache lines and 4 KiB pages, and Apple Silicon has 128-byte lines and 16 KiB pages.

Fixed-width extents remove four varint decodes from the paged hit path, worth 1.37x (694 -> 508 ns) at 10M keys. This is the same defect hash+flatfixed found in hash+flat, applied to the layout the frontier actually points at. Pinned to full: the paged layouts only separate at 10M keys; at ci scale everything fits in cache and a 100k-key extent varint-encodes to a single byte, so the arm being tested barely differs from the other. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

The same change is worth 1.59x on ordered scans (5.10 -> 3.22 ns/entry), which matters more than the hit figure: F9.5 fails because no composite scans as fast as the heap index, and this closes most of that gap. Pinned to full: the paged layouts only separate at 10M keys; at ci scale everything fits in cache and a 100k-key extent varint-encodes to a single byte, so the arm being tested barely differs from the other. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

A miss fails at the key comparison and never reaches the extent, so an encoding change behind that comparison must not move it. This is a harness check, not a performance claim -- if it ever stops holding, distrust P1 rather than celebrating it. Pinned to full: the paged layouts only separate at 10M keys; at ci scale everything fits in cache and a 100k-key extent varint-encodes to a single byte, so the arm being tested barely differs from the other. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

The same change on the MPH arm is worth 1.19x (788 -> 662 ns). Much less than the hash arm, because a BBHash lookup probes several level bit-arrays before it reaches the record, so the varint is a smaller share of a longer path. Pinned to full: the paged layouts only separate at 10M keys; at ci scale everything fits in cache and a 100k-key extent varint-encodes to a single byte, so the arm being tested barely differs from the other. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

1.61x on ordered scans (5.36 -> 3.32 ns/entry), essentially the same as the hash arm, because the scan path is the blob and is shared. Pinned to full: the paged layouts only separate at 10M keys; at ci scale everything fits in cache and a 100k-key extent varint-encodes to a single byte, so the arm being tested barely differs from the other. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

The mechanism check, as above. The MPH arm makes it sharper: its misses are dominated by the MPH probe itself, so a moved miss figure here would be unambiguous evidence of a harness fault. Pinned to full: the paged layouts only separate at 10M keys; at ci scale everything fits in cache and a 100k-key extent varint-encodes to a single byte, so the arm being tested barely differs from the other. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

The whole point of the format. 5M keys open in 0.29ms against 738ms, 2537x, because a mapped index validates a header instead of decoding every key and hashing the result. This is what moved F2.2 from failing to holding. Pinned to full: the arms only separate at scale -- at 50k keys the open difference is 61x rather than 2537x and the read difference is inside noise. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

Decoded 226 B/key resident against a mapped section of 99 B/key at 5M keys (the previous record: 186 against 67). The section is exactly what the flat index's plan says it is: 26.8 B of hash slots (2^24 slots for 5M keys, the power-of-two rounding at its worst), 12 B of directory with `index_inserts` room, 60 B of records under the half-again slack -- 98.8 predicted, 98.9 measured, with format v5's count field 6 B of it. Measured against the section rather than against resident size because a read pass faults in block and cache pages common to both arms and dilutes the difference: on that measure it reads 168 B/key against 226.

Point reads are 1893ns against 2334ns, 1.25x, so the space is not being spent to stand still. Much smaller than the 6.9x the ci profile reported, which was a small-store artifact. Pinned to full: the arms only separate at scale -- at 50k keys the open difference is 61x rather than 2537x and the read difference is inside noise. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

The price, and it is accepted deliberately: 394MB becomes 683MB at 5M keys, +73.5%, because a section read in place cannot be compressed. Space is the axis this engine has to spare and open latency is the one it does not. Measured on the minimal file -- one checkpoint -- because the churned file also contains holes left by reclaimed sections, which is a different quantity and was what made the first run of this report +217%. Pinned to full: the arms only separate at scale -- at 50k keys the open difference is 61x rather than 2537x and the read difference is inside noise. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

Zero bytes per key of permanent growth per checkpoint, on both arms. It was 9.2 and 66.9 respectively, forever: every checkpoint appended keys, blocks and reuse-log sections and released none of them. A pre-existing leak that the flat format made expensive enough to notice, and the reason this format was not turned on by default until it was fixed. Pinned to full: the arms only separate at scale -- at 50k keys the open difference is 61x rather than 2537x and the read difference is inside noise. Pinned to x86_64: measured on 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages.

Turning block compression off makes point reads 3.6x faster. The question was whether decompression explains any of LMDB's 2.9x read lead; it explains more than all of it. Pinned to full: at ci scale the store fits in cache and the space saving looks four times larger than it is. Pinned to x86_64.

And ordered scans 30x faster. A scan walks whole blocks in order, so it pays decompression on every one; this is the largest single effect measured anywhere in this suite. Pinned to full: at ci scale the store fits in cache and the space saving looks four times larger than it is. Pinned to x86_64.

The space given up is 1.04x -- 3017 MB against 3142 MB. Compression is buying almost nothing here because the payload is half-random by construction; a more compressible payload would save more, but the read and scan costs above do not depend on how well the data compresses. Pinned to full: at ci scale the store fits in cache and the space saving looks four times larger than it is. Pinned to x86_64.

Compression costs the write path too: 3.8x. It is off by default as of this measurement, so this claim now records what the option costs anyone who turns it back on rather than what the engine does. It stays expected-to-fail because the statement is about the compressor, not the default: paying on writes as well as reads and scans, for four percent of disk, is not a trade. Pinned to full: at ci scale the store fits in cache and the space saving looks four times larger than it is. Pinned to x86_64.

fsync is the dominant cost of publishing, by a wide margin: 415 ops/s against 12,985 without, 31.3x, on the read-your-writes shape. Every such operation costs a checkpoint because Store has no read method, and a checkpoint syncs twice. This is the whole of the gap on the workloads Supdb is worst at -- YCSB A/B/D/E/F sit at 0.07-0.14x of LMDB while C, which never publishes, sits at 1.73x. Recorded as expected-to-fail because the statement is about where the time goes, and it goes here. Pinned to full and to x86_64. The ratio is a property of this disk as much as of the engine -- a device with a faster flush would show less -- which is exactly why it is recorded as a measurement rather than folded into a design argument.

And it is worth far more than the largest thing an instruction profile could see. Callgrind put the block table decode at 34% of all instructions; mapping it removed 4.75x of the total instruction count and moved throughput by nothing, because the workload waits on a syscall. This claim exists to keep that lesson attached to a number: an instruction profile answers where the CPU goes, not why a workload is slow. Pinned to full and to x86_64. The ratio is a property of this disk as much as of the engine -- a device with a faster flush would show less -- which is exactly why it is recorded as a measurement rather than folded into a design argument.

The mapped block table costs nothing on a scan: 13,717,970 entries/s mapped against 13,748,135 owned, ratio 1.002 at p=0.70. This experiment exists because a scan resolves a block for every entry it walks, and the change that introduced the mapping was measured only on point reads -- one lookup, one resolve. The reasoning was sound and the answer is still no. Recorded so the next person who suspects this structure finds it already asked.

The mapped block table costs nothing on a point read either: 1,996,309 ops/s against 1,995,093, ratio 0.999 at p=0.90. Kept alongside F14.1 so the two are read together -- the point of the pair is that a structure can be free on one access pattern and not on another, and here it happens to be free on both.

Holding the current block across a scan's entries is worth 1.201x at 1M keys (17,342,159 against 14,441,442 entries/s, p=0.0022). A scan walks keys in rank order and consecutive keys usually share a block, so resolving one per entry re-reads the block table, re-bounds-checks the mapping and re-tests a checksum bit to learn what the previous entry already established. Finding it also turned up that the block was resolved *twice* per entry, since `check_extent` resolved it and then the read resolved it again; that fix is in both arms, so this figure understates what the work was worth. Worth recording that this is the sort of cost an instruction profile can see and a syscall-blind one cannot -- the exact opposite of the fsync case in f13.

Leaving the index slack as a hole is worth 1.077x on a bulk load (1,158,872 against 1,075,715 ops/s, p=0.0325) and 10.2% fewer bytes to the device (F16.2). It took 21 repetitions to say that. At the default seven it read 1.158x at p=0.0553 and then 1.132x at p=0.0409 on consecutive runs -- a verdict flipping without the engine changing, because the effect is around 10% and the repetition-to-repetition IQR is 17-19%. An underpowered measurement is not a cheap one, it is one that could not see, and the fix was more samples rather than a softer claim.

Both arms produce a 176,681,680-byte file, and send 157,949,952 against 175,951,872 bytes to the device -- 18MB, 10.2% fewer, for the same store. The flat index reserves half its record region again as slack so an in-place checkpoint has somewhere to put a lengthened record; nothing reads that region until an update writes into it, and an unwritten hole reads back as the same zeroes. This is exactly the pair CLAUDE.md means by measuring write amplification from /proc/self/io rather than inferring it from file size: file size cannot see a hole, and here the two answers differ by 18MB.

Borrowing the keys instead of copying them does not measurably speed up a bulk load: 1,181,333 ops/s against 1,147,204, ratio 1.030 at p=0.2502. The change is kept -- it allocates nothing where it used to allocate once per key, a million 16-byte mallocs at this scale -- but it is not a speedup and this entry says so. What sent me looking was a phase split showing the checkpoint as 820ms of a 1,443ms load while writing 57MB, where the flush had just written 101MB in 226ms; after the change a rerun showed 440ms. That 1.9x was drift. Two single runs on this machine differ by more than the change did, which is the whole reason arms go behind a runtime flag and run interleaved -- and I wrote the flag *because* I did not trust the number, which is the only reason this is recorded correctly.

Narrowing a seek with the fence is worth 1.066x: 698ns against 744ns, p=0.0073. I predicted eight times that, and said so out loud before measuring. The reasoning was that a seek is twenty probes into a 36MB region and the fence replaces them with fourteen into 300KB. What it misses is that the *upper* levels of a binary search over a static array visit the same few addresses on every search and are therefore already cached -- the fence replaces exactly the probes that were cheap, and the expensive bottom levels remain. Verifying the fence's answer against two records, which is what makes it safe, eats into the rest.

On the workload the fence was built for -- 50-entry scans, the shape YCSB-E runs -- it is worth 1.092x: 15,909,949 against 14,570,849 entries/s, p=0.0022 with IQRs of 2.0% and 1.4%. This is the finding that decides whether the fence earns a format version, since a seek that got faster without moving a scan would not. 9% is real, repeated and far less than predicted; it is kept because it is positive and measured, not because it was expected.

WAS 'holds', now measured rather than fitted, and the margin does not survive the change: Supdb walks at 24.41 ns/entry against LMDB's 22.99, ratio 0.942 at p=0.5229. This flip is not the engine getting worse and not the experiment going blind -- it is the experiment starting to measure the quantity it names. The per-entry cost is now the difference quotient between scans of 200 and 400 entries, which is what 'the cost of one more entry' means; it was the slope of a least-squares line fitted over lengths 1..400, across a range where the marginal cost of an entry falls from about 89ns to 15 before settling near 20. On this coefficient the fit was nearly right, and its problem was never arithmetic: it reported p=0.0409 for a margin the direct measurement cannot find at all. Across two runs an hour apart this ratio reads 1.018 and 0.942, crossing parity in both directions, no difference each time. Supdb and LMDB walk a scan at the same speed as far as this host can resolve.

FIXED, in the sense that the loss was never really measured: Supdb's shortest scan costs 857 ns against LMDB's 924, ratio 1.079 at p=0.6093, no difference. The old value -- 952 ns against 812, 0.853x at p=0.0022, a confident loss -- was the intercept of a straight line fitted over scan lengths 1..400, and that line is refuted by its own data. Its intercept lands ABOVE the measured cost of a one-entry scan for every engine in the suite and in every run since: +330ns for Supdb, +143 for LMDB, +9 for redb here, and +279/+208/+174 an hour earlier. A per-scan constant greater than the cheapest scan ever observed is not a constant, and two engines' versions of it are not a comparison. The floor is now read straight off the n=1 point with no model, and reads 0.947x and 1.079x across two runs -- across parity in both directions, where the fitted version said 0.853x at p=0.0022. With EXT.7 this removes the 'faster walker, larger constant' story entirely: both halves were fit artifacts pointing in opposite directions, and neither axis separates the two engines. full_range_fit is kept in every ext-sweep record so the refuted model stays visible rather than merely deleted, and src/bench/stats.rs carries the curve that refutes it as a test.

Verifying block checksums costs 0.715x on a cold scan -- 39,251,416 entries/s against 54,902,165 unverified, p=0.0022 with IQRs of 4.5% and 4.6%. f8-checksums measured this cost at 'read -1.0%, no difference' and that measurement was not wrong, it was on the wrong workload: a reader checks each block once and records it, so a point-read workload reads every block many times and amortises the check away. A scan over a fresh reader touches each block for the first time and pays for all of them. The amplification is the point -- a 64KiB block is checksummed in full to hand back a 100-byte value.

A scan's first pass costs 1.65x its steady state with verification on, and 1.09x with it off, so the cold penalty is the checksum and almost nothing else. The cold pass took 0 major faults and spent 0.0% of its wall time off CPU, which rules out page faults and I/O: this is CPU spent on CRC32C. That resolves the disagreement between ext-sweep, which discards a warmup and finds Supdb faster than LMDB at every scan length from 100 up, and ext-kv, which measures the first pass and finds it slower at exactly 100. Both are right about what they measure, and the difference between them is a guarantee LMDB does not offer -- Features::checksums is false for it.

Verifying a chunk instead of a block makes no difference to a cold scan that sweeps the store uniformly: 39,663,014 entries/s against 40,341,188, ratio 0.983 at p=0.3067. This is the prediction failing on arithmetic I should have done first. Verifying every chunk of a block *is* verifying the block -- the same bytes hashed -- so chunking cannot save anything on a workload that reaches all of them. It only helps a read that touches part of a block and does not come back. f19-coldscan measured the cold penalty as a CRC over everything the scan reads, and a uniform sweep reads everything.

A uniform cold pass still costs 1.44x its steady state per chunk, against 1.47x per block, because on that workload the two hash the same bytes. F19.2 measured 1.65x for whole blocks and this does not close it. What closes it for a uniform sweep is not a smaller verification unit -- there isn't one -- it is verifying less often or not at all, which is what ReadOptions::verify_checksums is for.

On a skewed scan workload -- Zipfian keys, which is what YCSB runs and what real access looks like -- chunk verification is worth 1.162x: 55,285,646 entries/s against 47,589,779, p=0.0022. This is the regime where a scan touches part of a block and moves on, so hashing 4KiB instead of 64KiB is a real saving. It took two attempts. The first measured 0.908x -- chunking made it *slower* -- because whole-block verification is checked once per block-resolve and amortised over the ~600 entries in it, while per-chunk was checked per extent: the same trick f15-scancache needed, and holding the last verified chunk across entries is what turned a 0.908x loss into a 1.162x win. YCSB-E moved from 0.48x of LMDB to 0.57x.

FIXED. The writer's read path now verifies what the reader's verifies: 0/8 damaged trials read through `Store::read_all` returned wrong bytes, where every one of them did before. `Store::read_all` was added so a writer could read its own writes without a checkpoint -- it took the mixed YCSB workloads from 0.07x of LMDB to 18x -- and went from the mapping to the caller with no checksum in between, so the same store answered with two guarantees depending on the handle. C1.2 said 'a read returns the bytes that were written, or an error' and every trial behind it opened a `Reader`; its statement now names the reader and this asks the same question of the other path. RocksDB verifies every block it loads by default, which is the bar being matched here. f21-writerverify prices it at 1.135x on a cold read pass and 0.956x warm, and `Options::verify_reads` is the knob for a caller who wants LMDB's trade instead -- LMDB has no checksums at all.

Verifying the writer's own reads costs 1.135x on a cold pass -- 1,417,715 ops/s against 1,608,870, p=0.0022 with IQRs of 0.9% and 3.8%. That is the price of the guarantee RocksDB charges by default and LMDB does not offer, on the path YCSB A through F read through. It was paid: A is 14.96x of LMDB with verification on where it was 17.69x with it off, C is 1.19x where it was 1.29x, and every ordering held.

A warm read pays 0.956x for verification -- almost nothing. A chunk is checked once and remembered, so the cost belongs to the first touch of a block rather than to the read path, which is exactly why f8-checksums measured warm point reads and found the whole thing free. Two experiments, the same mechanism, opposite-looking answers, and neither is wrong.

Scanning through the writer is worth 1.593x against opening a `Reader` for it: 35,123,371 entries/s against 22,043,018, p=0.0022 with IQRs of 2.6% and 6.1%. The shape is the kv suite's -- read through `Store::read_all`, then scan -- and the reader loses because it duplicates a mapping the writer already has and starts a verified bitset the writer has already filled, so it re-verifies a store this process just wrote. At ci there is no difference, because a cache-resident store has nothing to warm. This needed an arm: between two suite runs an hour apart both engines' scan throughput roughly doubled, so no cross-run number could have shown it.

The precondition, and the reason this experiment exists in this shape: 1,414,698,744 bytes of store against a 512MB cap, ratio 2.64. f1-outofcore reaches the same condition by building 23GB on a machine with more RAM than this one has, which is why F1.2 is not_exercised at every profile below full and unrunnable here at all -- 15GB of RAM and 20GB of free disk cannot produce it. Out-of-core is a ratio, not a size, and a memory cgroup makes the ratio a parameter of the experiment instead of a property of the host. Page cache is charged to the cgroup that faults it in, so capping the cgroup caps the cache.

The default readahead amplifies an out-of-core random read by 86,977x: 8,697,724 device bytes to return a 100-byte value, against 14,149 with MADV_RANDOM. Passing no advice means MADV_NORMAL, so every miss faults in a cluster of pages on the assumption that a read is the start of a sequential run. For a random point read that is wrong twice -- it fetches a window to return a hundred bytes, and the pages it fetched speculatively evict pages something was still using, so they are fetched again. Measured from /proc/self/io with the page cache dropped before each pass, so these are bytes the device was asked for rather than bytes inferred from file size.

Telling the kernel a random read is random is worth 25.2x out of core: 5,143 reads/s against 204, p=0.0022. The 204 is the point -- F1.2 records 370 reads/s out-of-core against 338,681 resident and blames an engine with no madvise anywhere, and this reproduces that collapse at a sixteenth of the scale and then removes most of it with one syscall. It is regime-dependent and the opposite way round when the store fits: resident and uncapped, MADV_RANDOM is about 15x *slower*, because readahead is a working prefetcher when the pages it fetches survive. That is why `Readahead` is a knob and why the default is unchanged; an adaptive `Auto` is the obvious follow-up and has not been measured, so it does not exist yet.

`Readahead::Auto` picks the faster advice at every swept ratio where the two differ by more than the noise floor. At 1M keys the default is 3.2-3.4x ahead from a ratio of 0.05 up to 1.00, and behind by 1.7x at 1.25, 6.5x at 1.50 and 28x at 3.00; Auto tracks the switch. The threshold took three attempts and the experiment caught both wrong ones. 0.5 looked conservative and advised Random across the whole 0.5-1.0 band where the default is three times faster. 1.0 sat exactly on the common case -- a cgroup rounds its limit down to a page multiple, so a store sized to its memory comes out a couple of kilobytes over and takes the wrong branch, which the sweep duly caught at ratio 1.00. 1.1 clears it.

The same threshold mispicks on a smaller store, and this entry exists so that is on the record rather than hidden by a profile that is never cited. At 556MB the crossover is around 0.75 rather than 1.25, so `Auto` keeps the default advice at 0.75 and 1.00 where Random is 8-16% ahead. The crossover moves with store size because what actually decides it is access density -- how much of the store a workload touches -- and a single constant over the file-to-memory ratio cannot express that. The constant is tuned where it costs the most: mispicking at ci is worth 16%, picking right at full is worth 3.3x.

My statement was that readahead stops paying somewhere below a file-to-memory ratio of 1. It does not: at 1M keys MADV_RANDOM first overtakes the default at 1.25. Readahead keeps paying right up to and past the point where the store no longer fits, because the pages it fetches speculatively are still being used before they are evicted. Recorded as failing rather than reworded, because it is the sentence that produced two wrong thresholds.

At 556MB the crossover is 0.75, below 1 -- so the same claim holds here and fails at full. That disagreement is the finding: the crossover is not a constant of the engine, it moves with store size, and any single threshold is a compromise across scales rather than a law. Pinned to both profiles deliberately so the pair cannot be read as one answer.

A damaged store is refused by `Store::open` or read correctly, never opened onto: 0/24 damaged files were accepted and then disagreed with what was written, and 2 were refused outright. This matters more than an ordinary read path because reopening rebuilds the block table, the key tables and every reference count from the file, and then *writes on top of* whatever it believed. Building it found a live defect: `Appender::read_extent` indexed `self.blocks[e.block]` unchecked and took the process down on a damaged index. `Reader` has had `loc_of` for exactly that since a damaged file panicked through `scan`; the writer's copy had never been asked, because nothing could reopen a store to ask it. That is the shape of this whole entry: the limitation prevented the test of the limitation.

Supdb loads at 199,485 ops/s against LMDB's 572,416 when both commit per batch -- 0.348x at p=0.0022 in the canonical record; the same night's other full-suite readings were 0.298x, 0.361x and 0.271x (the comparator moved 1.6% between those pairs while Supdb's own arm moved 26%, so the residual instability is ours and is recorded rather than averaged away). The session arc on this axis: 6,735 ops/s (91x behind, 270x write amplification), 54,333 after in-place index insertion, 152,790 after log-first single-fsync points, ~200,000 now that the log carries the VALUES and a durability point seals nothing -- blocks are written later, full, on the store's own schedule, and the device sees ~834 MB per load against 1,459 before. Each step was predicted by a decomposition before it was built, and the last one was nearly refuted by its own gate: at 1M keys the first value-log walked every key per point looking for unlogged bytes, an O(keys^2) tax that read 0.149x until the per-shard queue removed it (f36 at 1M: 0.718x values-vs-extents unfixed, 1.814x fixed -- both runs kept). Still 3.4x behind, so still failing; what remains is per-batch arena append + fsync + block-table section against LMDB's single page-chain commit, and the macOS barrier ladder now brackets that floor from both sides: 0.426x pre-value-log, 0.490x/0.487x with it, replicated to 0.4% (+19.3% where Linux gained +30.6%, the compression being F_FULLFSYNC's share), leaving a 2.04x residual with both engines paying exactly one barrier per batch.

The load axis finally has a host that can read it. On this x86 VM the entry is unmeasurable -- lmdb-nosync, untouched, moved 85% between consecutive runs, and the ratio has read 0.53x to 1.06x with no code change. The Mac runner (results/apple-silicon/ext-kv-buffered-pair.run*.json) measures the pair twice with each engine drifting no more than 1.5% between runs: 0.857x at p=0.0073 and 0.852x at p=0.1599 -- the point estimate stable to 0.6%, one run clearing the gate and one not, which is what a ~15% effect at the edge of resolution looks like. So the sequential arrival deficit is real and it is 14-15%, not the 47% this host's drift suggested. Arrival order still decides the sign: shuffled keys win 1.94x (EXT.13). Architecture caveat: aarch64, 128-byte lines, 16KiB pages; this claim's pinned record stays x86 and stays failing until an x86 host that holds still says otherwise.

Holding, quoted as a range: 1,325,496 reads/s against lmdb's 917,928, 1.444x at p=0.0022, on the recovered host state -- after 1.262x and 1.379x on the degraded one and a tie at 1.043x before that. The old engine's read lead over lmdb across six runs is 1.196x, 1.092x, 1.043x, 1.379x, 1.262x, 1.444x: real, and it moves with the host. The read claim the project carries is the next engine's (EXT.23).

Back inside the noise, hours after clearing the gate: tonight's two canonical runs read 1.155x at p=0.0298 and then 0.934x at p=0.31, and the axis's x86 history is 1.046x (nd), 1.155x (sig), 0.934x (nd) -- a coin toss on this host, recorded as fails because the statement is 'scans faster' and the latest record cannot show it. The evidence that is not a coin toss is Apple Silicon: 1.174x and 1.178x with rel_iqr under 1.3%, replicated. When the two architectures disagree this cleanly on stability, quote the one that replicates and say which host a number came from.

NOT ESTABLISHED, across five full runs: 1.187x (p=0.0215), 1.050x, 1.021x, 1.007x and 1.035x, no difference in four of the five. The first is the one I wrote a claim from, and a marginal p from a single run is exactly the EXT.1 failure mode this repository already documents. The arena's bulk-load benefit does not exist at a size this host can resolve. What the arena does do is remove 50,305 live allocations per 50k keys and cut instructions 16% per key -- neither of which shows up as load throughput, which is itself the finding: this load is not instruction-bound.

Holds, but marginally, and the margin is falling: across five full runs the ratio has read 1.144x (p=0.0022), 1.117x, 1.079x, 1.028x and 1.083x, clearing the gate in four and missing it in the fifth at p=0.0553 -- a hair the wrong side of it. Read this as about 8% and fragile rather than as a result. It is still the workload where the arena could have lost outright, since an append must keep a key's run contiguous and copies it to the arena tail whenever another key has appended in between. Set against F25.3's 2.2x resident memory, an 8% append-path gain that flips one run in five is a poor trade, and the next thing to try is removing the up-front reservation rather than defending it.

The arena's price, now 197.2 MB against 132.7 MB for the same load -- 0.664x at p=0.0100, where it was 0.450x. It reserved each shard's whole `buffer_bytes` share on first use, on the theory that growth memcpys explained the 21% rise in last-level misses the arena caused. They did not: reserving removed every one of those copies and the misses did not move, so the reservation was the answer to a question it was not the answer to, and it cost 2.2x resident memory. It starts at 128KB and grows now, which recovered a third of the memory and changed neither the append gain (1.080x against 1.079x) nor the absent load gain. What remains is `Vec` doubling slack -- capacity up to twice length -- and a chunked arena would remove that too. Recorded as failing because 1.5x resident memory for an 8% append-path gain that flips one run in five (F25.2) is not yet a trade worth defending; it is a cost with a known next step.

1,834,782 ops/s at a 4MB buffer against 1,827,426 at 256MB -- 1.004x at p=0.7015, no difference -- while resident memory falls from 279.9 MB to 173.0, a 38% saving for nothing given up. All four arms (4, 16, 64, 256MB) are statistically tied on throughput, so the choice is free and smaller strictly dominates. The external adapter configures 256MB, which is larger than the 105MB dataset, so Supdb holds all of it -- and that is a straightforward part of why EXT.10 shows 218MB resident against LMDB's 46. This experiment could not have been run at all before `Options::seal_on_put`: `append` sealed when a shard's buffer filled and `put` never checked, so a put-only workload ignored `buffer_bytes` entirely and every arm here would have behaved identically. What is left after the fix is Supdb's key index, which stays resident through a load at roughly 57 bytes per key, and no buffer setting touches that.

Updating existing keys under Sync::Always runs 173,446 ops/s; inserting new ones runs 42,079 -- 4.122x at p=0.0022, on identical operation counts, identical checkpoint counts and the same durability policy. So durability is not what EXT.9's 0.010x is made of. Insertion under durability is. `checkpoint_in_place` edits the mapped index through slack instead of rewriting it, and opens with `if nkeys != meta.len() { return Ok(false) }` -- any key added or removed sends the checkpoint down the full-rewrite path, and every batch of a bulk load adds. The margin scales the way an O(key count) rewrite must: 1.067x at 20k keys, 3.282x at 100k, 4.122x at 200k. It is visible in device bytes too, 1,269.6 MB against 984.4 for the same work. This is the measurement that says where to spend: a durable Supdb is not slow, a *growing* durable Supdb is, and the in-place path already exists and is simply declined.

36.02 B/line between 50k and 250k lines against 36.13 between 250k and 1M -- 0.3% apart -- over a fixed cost of 632,616 bytes. The postings dominate and there is one per line per indexed field; the key count is bounded by field cardinalities, so it lands in the fixed term. This record was re-taken twice in one day for cause: the freelist class_of underflow (reported by logshed) had been inflating every sub-4KiB placement to 7,680 bytes since the format existed, and then redo_log defaulting on silently added a 4 MB log arena to every CLOSED store's file -- the fixed cost read 4,826,920 until close() learned to drop the arena it can never use. A closing store now trims it directly rather than releasing it into a free list whose coalescing rightly ignores generation-quarantined slots.

36.13 B/line over 632,616 fixed puts the 32 MB budget at 911,192 lines/day; a 10M-line day is 11 objects, each independently under budget and each skippable by a time-ranged query. This is what makes R2.2(a) -- an OPFS synchronous access handle over one downloaded object -- viable, and why the reader in blob.rs stays synchronous. The budget briefly read 795,104 lines while every closed store was shipping a 4 MB arena of reserved zeroes to the browser; see W1.1.

At 1M lines, line order writes 740,509,448 bytes where term order writes 40,957,384 -- 18.08x. Line order interleaves every key, so a hot key's run is sealed into many small extents and merge_threshold rewrites the whole run each time it crosses four; F5.1 records that as a latency tail and it shows up here as dead space. Term order seals each run once and merges zero times. The ratio was 22.6x when first measured; in-place index insertion (index_inserts) since made the line-order arm cheaper, which narrowed it without changing the verdict, and the design panel's rank-2 item (geometric deferred consolidation) exists to close most of the rest.

Flipped by format v5. Counting now costs 94 ns/probe against 2,345 to read, 24.8x at p=0.0022, because every extent carries its record count and `count` sums a field over the borrowed extent slice without touching a block. Before v5 the walk cost what reading cost (2,493 against 2,516 ns, 1.009x at p=1.0): skipping a payload does not skip the cache lines it sits in. The premise R4.3 was written on is true now, and it was bought rather than found: four bytes an extent, 25% on a 16-byte record, paid by every store.

Flipped by format v5, and recorded failing so the premise cannot come back the other way: a count that is O(extents) IS available from the extent list now, for any value width, and `count_fixed` -- the schema-dependent form that was 27.1x faster than the walk -- is a statistical tie with the general `count` (95 against 94 ns/probe, no difference at p=0.37). What made the fixed form special was that the extent list did not carry a count; it does now.

Restated with the format change made. Before v5 this gate priced a stored per-extent count at under 20 ns of saving over `count_fixed` and declined it as not worth four bytes an extent for logshed's fixed-width schema; the priority then changed to spending space for time and variable-width counts were wanted, so the bytes were paid. The gate now measures what they bought against the floor any count has, resolving the key and stopping: 94 ns/probe for the general count against 94 for the lookup, +0.7 ns, no difference at p=0.80. A general count costs a lookup.

Flipped by format v5: the general dictionary count no longer walks anything, so 'counting from the extent list is at least 10x walking it' has nothing left to beat -- `scan_counts` runs 4.5 ns/key against `scan_counts_fixed`'s 5.2 (0.868x for the fixed form, p=0.0022; the fixed form does a division and a `last` check per extent where the general one reads a field). Before v5 the ratio was 283x (1,226 against 4.3 ns/key). The capability this protected -- a browser ranking a whole dictionary without touching a block -- is now W2.5's, for any schema.

The general dictionary count is within 1.5x of the fixed-width one: 4.5 against 5.2 ns/key over 2,000 keys, so a day's term dictionary ranks in about 9 us through the schema-independent call, for values of any width. Before v5 the general form lost by 283x and only the fixed form was usable; W2.4 records that flip.

R3.3 asks for a size budget stated up front and measured against. 64 KB gzipped, and the module is 41,010 (90,168 raw). The budget is five times logshed's entire 12 KB gzipped client, which sounds generous until W3.2: the first 12.7 KB of it is the Rust standard library's floor and is not reducible from this side. It is one round trip, it is immutable and cached so it is paid per deploy rather than per query, and it is 0.1% of the 32 MB index budget it exists to read. No binding generator -- the ABI is twenty hand-written C functions passing integers and byte ranges, because a generator's shim and descriptor sections are exactly what this budget is about.

A blob measured alone cannot say whether it is large because supdb is large or because a Rust cdylib on wasm starts out large, and those want different responses. `web/floor/` is the control: same profile, same standard-library surface (Vec, String, format!, std::io::Error, a fallible entry point), none of supdb. It is 12,670 bytes gzipped, so the floor is 31% of what ships and supdb's marginal cost is 28,340. Worth knowing before optimising: dropping lz4 from the wasm build -- which would make a compressed file unreadable in the browser -- was tried and saved 2,717 gzipped bytes, about a tenth, so it was not taken.

28,095 bytes gzipped above the floor against a 32 KB ceiling. This is the number that moves when the reader grows, where W3.1 is the number the user pays; separating them means a change that adds reader surface is visible here even though W3.1 would still have room. It has now moved once, exactly as intended: R6's planning seam -- supdb_open_probe, supdb_open_plan, supdb_ranges, and the redo-log emptiness check behind them -- cost 4,225 gzipped bytes, 23,870 to 28,095; fixing Blob::verify's poisoned bitmap (a failed checksum marked the chunk verified, so the error fired once and the next read served the corrupt bytes -- tests/blob.rs and web/test/node.mjs pin it now) cost 245 more, to 28,340, leaving 4,428 of headroom. The next reader feature pays against that remainder or argues for a new ceiling in the open.

R6.2's whole design rests on this: a lookup consults only resident sections, so the byte ranges a read will touch are known before any data byte moves, and JavaScript can fetch them asynchronously while the read stays synchronous -- no Asyncify, no JSPI, no fault-and-retry. That only works if the plan is *exact*, so it is measured rather than argued: a recording byte source logs every (offset, length) the reader pulls, and at full, 7 day-index probes and 7 segment probes each read exactly what `ranges_for` named -- for `read_all` and for the walked `count`, with an absent key planning and reading nothing, and `ranges_for_many` equal to the union of its keys' reads. The granularity that makes it true is the stored block, not the extent: `with_extent` fetches whole blocks (verification and decompression want the enclosing bytes), so a plan at extent granularity would under-report, which is the first trap the test was built around. `tests/ranges.rs` holds the same property on every push, including through compressed blocks and for `open_ranges` against the open's own reads.

W2.2 and W2.4 priced the extent-arithmetic counts in nanoseconds; over a caching byte source the same property becomes bytes never fetched, and that is measured, not inferred: at full, count_fixed, stored_bytes and a scan_counts_fixed over the whole 104-key segment dictionary made 0 source reads, where the walked count of the same 7 probe keys reads 2,015,000 bytes. This is what lets a browser rank a segment's whole term dictionary -- the breakdown panels -- over ranged HTTP with nothing fetched beyond the open, and it is why the browser test asserts fetchedBytes does not move across the counts and the scan.

What R6 buys, in bytes, on the shape logshed actually rolls: a segment's dictionary is bounded by field cardinality (~104 keys however much traffic), so at full the open fetches 19,832 bytes of a 31,384,960-byte object -- superblock probe, key index, block table -- and the 7-probe query set plans 2,015,000 more: 6.5% fetched, the rest never leaves object storage. The day shape reads 11.0% of 9,651,504. Both denominators are honest ones: the class_of underflow and the retained 4 MB log arena were fixed before these numbers were taken, which cost the percentages about a point against the inflated files they replaced. The browser test carries the same result end to end in Chromium: a 512 KiB cache over ranged HTTP against a 3,187,648-byte segment file that is 98% data, answers identical to the native reader's, total fetched under the data region alone, and the budget observed to evict. The premise -- index and block table fetched whole at open -- is priced in that 19,832 and expires when key cardinality does: a trigram or free-text index would need the index fetched sparsely too, which changes the JS host only, because every range in the ABI is an absolute file offset.

FIXED twice over. The extents-only log earned 1.440x against the best non-log arm; now that the log carries values -- a durability point appends unsealed bytes and seals nothing -- it earns 2.977x (p=0.0022): logged 327,603 ops/s at write amplification 3.58x against rewriting at 110,038 and 34.58x, 79 MB to the device against 765. The history of this claim tracked the design's whole arc: 5.112x against naive rewrites, 1.116x once index_inserts made the rewrite arm fast, 1.440x when points went log-first, and 3.022x when the seal left the durability point entirely. F29.2's guarantee is unchanged at 500/500, now covering value records: a fresh reader serves bytes straight from the arena overlay, and tests/valuelog.rs holds the crash-reopen contract -- deltas concatenate, replacements hide sealed state, deletes win over values, and a reopen never re-logs what the arena already holds.

FIXED, and on by default: 500 of 500 keys that a logged checkpoint made durable are visible to a reader opened before the next full rewrite, where it was 0 of 500. A `Reader` replays the log at open and merges it over the published index. The index itself is untouched -- it is mapped, shared between processes and read in place, and none of that survives being edited per reader -- so a record whose key exists replaces its extents and moves nothing, and one whose key is new takes a rank and shifts every published rank at or after it. `keys`, `seek` and `scan` see the merged order, and the fast path that walks the mapped section by rank stands down whenever there is anything to merge. Turning it on then exposed a reclamation bug older than the log: `live_key_off` was maintained only inside the flat branch and only when the index could be adopted for in-place editing, so with the varint layout it stayed None, the pruning loop saw a key section that did not match 'the live one', and released it. That was survivable while every checkpoint rewrote the key section -- the previous one really was superseded -- and the log makes a section outlive its generation. The next block table was then placed on top of the index every reader was using, which surfaced as lz4 failing on a section nobody had written there.

139,402 ops/s against 29,112 -- 4.788x at p=0.0022 -- for a workload that only inserts, with 1.85x fewer device bytes (509.8 MB against 944.5). It scales the way avoiding an O(key count) rewrite must: 1.582x at 20k keys, 3.254x at 100k, 4.788x at 200k. `checkpoint_in_place` declined every insertion outright, and f27 priced that refusal at 4.122x -- which is what this recovers, to within the noise. The records and the hash always had room for a new key; only the directory did not, because it is a sorted array and growing it shifts everything after. It is double-buffered now, so the spliced copy goes into the buffer nobody is reading and one aligned store of `dir_state` publishes which is live and how many keys it holds -- the same discipline the record path already used, where the bytes go down first and a single store publishes them.

52.56 MB against 385.21 -- the file is 7.33x SMALLER with room to insert, at p=0.0001, and the prediction was the opposite. Doubling the directory costs about 4 bytes per key on an index that is about 57, and Supdb already loses the size axis to LMDB (EXT.6), so this claim was written expecting to have to defend a size regression. It does not: rewriting the index for every insertion appends a fresh section each time and reclaims them more slowly than they accumulate, which costs far more than the second buffer ever could. The reserved directory is the smaller half of a trade whose larger half nobody had measured.

Supdb loads a shuffled key set at 584,090 ops/s against lmdb-nosync's 192,245 -- 3.038x at p=0.0022 -- where the same run has it at 0.199x on the same keys arriving in order (314,576 against 1,577,594). The run before read 2.785x shuffled and 0.305x ordered. A swing of 15x on arrival order alone, with the engines, the guarantees and the key set identical. EXT.10 measured only the ordered arm, and the suite has been reading it as a statement about loads. Both arms are real: ordered arrival is a common shape and Supdb is 5x behind on it. What changes is that the comparison now says which shape it is about. lmdb-nosync is still transactional, so read this as a bound.

Supdb loads at 314,576/s in order and 584,090 shuffled -- a factor of 0.54, so faster out of order (0.89 in the run before). LMDB goes 1,577,594 to 192,245, a factor of 8.21, and 658,292 to 48,041 when durable, a factor of 13.7 (8.10 and 13.9 the run before). The next engine sits between them: 429,659 to 284,938, a factor of 1.51 -- it sorts at seal and merges what it cannot promote, so it keeps some of the B-tree's preference for order and none of its collapse. That is the architectural difference rather than a ranking: a B-tree taking keys in order fills pages left to right and splits almost never, and the same tree taking them shuffled splits constantly, while an append-structured store writes where the cursor already is either way. It is the property Supdb should have and the first measurement here that shows it, and it is worth more than either ordering, because a store whose ingest rate does not depend on what the keys look like is one you can size capacity for.

Shuffled, the next engine loads 284,938 ops/s against lmdb's 48,041 -- 5.931x at p=0.0022 -- with both committing per batch and both transactional, so nothing leans. shape-plan.md registered the opposite: P27.1 put this arm at 0.35x to 0.55x, reasoning from the next engine's own cost of merging what promotion cannot route. That half was right -- its ordered arm in the same run is 429,659, 0.653x of lmdb and bracketing EXT.22's 0.694x from the other suite, and its swing is 1.508x (P27.2, P27.3 held). What the plan missed is lmdb's swing: 658,292 to 48,041, 13.7x, because a durable commit of 1,000 random keys dirties about as many leaf pages and the fsync writes them all, where 1,000 ascending keys dirty a handful. The canonical load's ascending keys are the one arrival order that flatters the B-tree; on the other, the matched durable load is not close. Quote this with EXT.22, never instead of it.

It does not: put 0.434s (42.4%), flush 0.136s (13.3%), checkpoint 0.453s (44.3%) for 1M keys arriving in order. Building the key index is the largest phase of a bulk load, and it costs 3.3x more than the flush that writes 105MB of actual data -- so it is the sort and the encode, not I/O. This is where EXT.13's 3.3x loss on ordered arrival lives. Two earlier readings were wrong about it and are worth keeping: cachegrind reports 62x LMDB's last-level misses per key on this shape, which reads like a scattered write path, and I took it for one -- but the same profile puts 1% of those misses in the hash probe and the rest in `checkpoint_inner`, `seal_shard` and the memcpy inside them. Timed directly, Supdb's put path is within 1.17x of LMDB's; the whole gap is the flush. A miss count says where the misses are, not which phase is slow. This is the same fixed cost that makes Supdb indifferent to arrival order (EXT.14), so it is the price of that property rather than an oversight -- but it is embarrassingly parallel across 64 shards and is done on one thread, which is the obvious thing to try next.

Inside a 0.468s checkpoint over 1M keys: sort 0.067s, encode 0.086s, crc 0.009s, pwrite 0.015s, fsync 0.186s. Building the index is 33% and making it durable is 40%, and neither is the one thing to remove. That is the finding, because three separate profiles each looked like it was. cachegrind reported 62x LMDB's last-level misses per key on an ordered load, which reads like a scattered write path -- `cg_annotate` puts 1% of them in the hash probe. The phase that looked like a 57MB section write took 4.7x what a bare 57MB write costs on this machine, which is 0.087s measured against a control, and that gap is what finally exposed the `sync_data` sitting inside the phase; the pwrite it appeared to be is 3% of the checkpoint. And f32 refuted preallocation, which had been the explanation for the write being slow, by aiming at disk blocks when the cost was never there. Against LMDB's 0.49s for the same load, Supdb's excess splits roughly evenly between building an index LMDB does not have and flushing the 1.33x bytes that index adds -- one root cause, two costs, and no single phase to delete.

1,145,201 ops/s with the varint index against 816,259 with the flat one -- 1.403x at p=0.0022 -- with the file at 105.5 MB against 168.6 and the checkpoint at 0.342s against 0.663s, of which fsync is 0.132s against 0.233s. This is f31's flush half tested directly: it said the excess over LMDB splits between building an index LMDB does not have and flushing the bytes that index adds, and removing 37% of those bytes moves the load by 1.4x. The lever is real and it is the only one that hits both halves at once, because the same bytes are what the sort and the encode produce and what the fsync then has to push. Note it is not free and not a recommendation on its own: see F33.2.

1,884,035 reads/s flat against 1,906,483 varint -- 0.988x at p=0.6365, no difference at 1M keys. F11.3 measures 1.25x for the flat index at 5M keys and both are right: the heap index it replaces costs 186 bytes per key resident, which is 930MB at 5M keys and comfortable at 1M. So the flat index's read advantage arrives with scale, while its costs are paid at every size -- 1.403x on a bulk load (F33.1) and +73.5% on the file (F11.4). Recorded as failing because a layout chosen for reads that does not help reads at the size being measured is a cost with no return there, and the honest conclusion is not that the flat index is wrong but that fixing it at compile time is: this is the same shape as `Readahead::Auto`, which picks by file-to-memory ratio rather than being set once.

0.087s against 0.1678s -- 1.930x at p=0.0009 on four cores, for the whole index build. Every part of it is threaded: the sort splits and merges (0.079s to 0.051s); the record loop splits because `rec_offs` is a prefix sum, so a range of keys owns a contiguous range of record bytes and its directory entries are `i*4`, disjoint by construction (0.035s to 0.012s); and the hash claims slots with compare-exchange (0.069s to 0.035s). The hash was two thirds of the encode and the last part done, which is why the first version of this claim measured only 1.253x -- parallelising the visible half of a phase and stopping is how an inch gets left behind. Below 64k keys none of it engages: threads cost more than the work, and small checkpoints are the common case.

995,460 ops/s against 957,516 -- 1.040x at p=0.2502, still no difference, with the build now 1.930x faster rather than 1.667x. It saves 0.081s of a 1.0s load, which is 8%, and this host cannot resolve 8% end to end: EXT.1 has moved 0.866x to 1.331x here with no code change at all. Recorded as failing because that is what the gate says, and the useful form of the result is the pair -- gate the phase, where 1.930x at p=0.0009 is unambiguous, and report the load contribution as arithmetic. An 8% saving that cannot be measured end to end on the available machine is still 8%; what it is not is evidence, and the two should not be confused. The Mac runner holds ratios to 1.2-5.0% across runs and could resolve it.

Supdb ranks the 2,000-key day dictionary at 9.22 ns/key against lmdb-dup's 35.09 -- 3.81x at p=0.0022, and 3.91x on the second run of the pair -- scan_counts_fixed against a NEXT_NODUP cursor plus mdb_cursor_count on a DUPSORT|DUPFIXED database, LMDB's genuinely best shape for this data. W2.4's 283x was this walk against Supdb's own varint decode; this is it against an engine that stores the count in its dup tree, and extent arithmetic on a mapped section still beats a B-tree step per key by 3.8x. The checksums-on arm measures 9.15 ns -- identical, because a fixed-stride count touches no block, which doubles as the rig's null check. lmdb-dup is still transactional, so read the win as a bound. Warm, like ext-sweep; EXT.12 owns cold.

count_fixed answers a point posting-count in 34.73 ns/probe against MDB_SET plus mdb_cursor_count's 257.7 -- 7.42x at p=0.0022, 7.43x on the paired run. W2.2's 27.1x was count_fixed against Supdb's own O(values) walk; this is it against an engine that stores the count, which is exactly the format change W2.3 priced at 14.9 ns for Supdb and declined. The declined four bytes per extent are not what separates the engines: the gap is one hash probe plus a division against a cursor descent.

Supdb intersects two terms' posting lists at 9,729 ns/pair against lmdb-dup's 7,486 -- 0.769x at p=0.0022 -- recorded as failing on purpose. Supdb's arm is the NAIVE decode-both merge: read_all both lists into reused buffers, then a two-pointer count, because the shipped read paths expose no streaming merge -- every posting is varint-decoded and copied before the merge sees it, where LMDB merges in place across GET_MULTIPLE pages and copies nothing. This entry prices the missing merge kernel; the rank-5 FixedRun work owns building it, and 0.769x is the number it has to move.

Reading one term's full posting list: 3.44 ns/posting against lmdb-dup's 1.06 -- 0.307x at p=0.0022. The baseline that keeps EXT.15 and EXT.16 honest, and the shape DUPFIXED is built for: 4-byte postings packed end to end, a page per GET_MULTIPLE call, no per-value work. Supdb pays a varint length prefix per posting -- a 5-byte stride for 4-byte data -- and the serial dependent decode W2.1 documents. Claimed as parity and it is not parity; the counts are where the format wins, not the bulk read. One consolation recorded because it is measured: Supdb's file is 5.02 MB against lmdb-dup's 7.33 for the same million postings -- the size axis, lost on ext-kv's 100-byte values, flips on 4-byte fixed-width ones.

FIXED, in two steps the three-arm decomposition now prices separately. Log-first points took the residual from 87.4% to 31.3% (fsync stopped flushing a 68 MB mapping's dirty pages); the value-carrying log then removed the seal from the point entirely and took the whole bill down: 79.2 MB reach the device for the log-values arm against 161.4 for log-extents and 765.1 for no-log, residual 19.1%. values_vs_extents reads 1.764x and values_vs_nolog 2.851x at 200k keys (p=0.0022; arms 339,332 / 192,425 / 119,014 ops/s at 79.2 / 157.0 / 765.1 MB); at 1M keys the same arms read 1.814x and 4.819x -- but only after an O(keys) scan per point was replaced by a per-shard queue, and the unfixed 1M run that read 0.718x is kept in results history as the shape of that quadratic. The ledger stays in the experiment so the next regression of this kind is a diff, not a hunt.

Deferred (geometric suffix) consolidation lifts fragmenting append throughput 3.963x over the inline whole-run merge (137,660 vs 34,734 ops/s, p=0.0022) -- ABOVE the 1.6-3.5x prediction band registered before the run, with the refutation floor at 1.3x. Inline rewrites O(n^2) bytes per key over its life; deferred absorbs an older extent only into a run at least its own size, so a byte is copied O(log n) times. Default ON since this record; the flag remains the measurement instrument.

Deferred consolidation shortens the append p99.9 3.427x: 501.8us inline to 146.4us deferred, worst single append 202.0ms to 70.1ms. This is F5.1's tail measured against the policy that causes it. Note what deferral does NOT do: the biggest cascade merge is still O(run) -- it bounds how often the big rewrites happen, not how big the biggest one is.

Recorded as failing ON PURPOSE: deferred consolidation taxes the read-back pass at 0.762x (30.98 vs 40.68 Mvalues/s), because a deferred key holds O(threshold + log n) extents where inline holds at most threshold, and reads pay per extent. This is the price of the 3.96x write-side win and this entry is what keeps it from being forgotten. The default flipped ON with this loss on the books; if a read-heavy deployment finds it unacceptable, the policy needs a list-length cap, and this entry is where that decision lives.

Inline sends 4,699.7 MB to the block layer where deferred sends 1,286.7, for 113.3 MB of appended records -- 3.652x fewer device bytes (p=0.0014). The O(n^2) rewrite is a device cost before it is a latency cost, which is how W1.3 saw it first on the space axis.

File after close: deferred 1,287.6 MB against inline 4,699.6 (0.274x, p=0.0004). The same mechanism read through the file: what inline rewrote and left dead, deferred never wrote. Downstream, flipping the default took w1's line-ordered day index from 740.5 MB to 190.0 -- the naive-roll penalty W1.3 prices fell from 22.6x to 5.17x while the claim itself kept holding, since term order still writes less than a third.

The unfiltered fan tax is linear and inside the band registered in fanout-plan.md before the run: 90ns per extra probe at four segments, 92 at sixteen (k1 554ns/read, fan4 689, fan16 1247, both p=0.0022). The ci smoke read 21-27ns and argued the band was too high; full scale restored it, because at 1M keys a failed hash probe misses cache like everything else. A per-segment existence filter earns its place only by adjudicating presence in well under 90ns; that number is now the filter's budget rather than a guess.

Segmentation itself is free: perfectly-routed reads over four and sixteen segments are indistinguishable from the single store (1.068x and 1.120x, p=0.0553, no difference -- leaning positive if anything, the ci run's smaller-index cache effect shrunk into noise at 1M keys). The entire fan-out cost is the probing, none of it the splitting, so the next engine buys write-side segmentation at zero read cost IF routing is solved -- and F38.1 prices what routing must beat.

Registered prediction P3 said the x86 read lead survives an unfiltered four-segment fan; it does not, and this entry records the refutation. fan4 keeps 80.5% of k1 (threshold was 85%), which puts EXT.11's 1.355x lead at 1.09x -- inside that comparison's own noise on this host -- and fan16 keeps 44.4%, lead 0.60x, gone outright. The design consequence is stronger than predicted: routing or filtering is required from k=4 up, not merely at large k. Read with F38.2, the shape is settled -- segments cost nothing, unrouted probes cost everything.

A raw log-only durable batch -- framed append + fdatasync, no engine -- sustains 1,191,125 ops/s at batch 1000 on this host, 0.84ms per barrier, inside the 600k-2.5M band registered in walfloor-plan.md. That is 2.08x LMDB's recorded durable load (EXT.9, 572,416, context only), so a one-barrier commit has the headroom to win the axis this engine has always lost; whether an engine can stay near its own floor is now the design question, not whether the floor is high enough.

Adding a hash-map insert per op -- the memtable bookkeeping no engine can skip -- keeps 85.1% of the raw floor (1,014,003 against 1,191,125, p=0.0298). The tax is real but small: the write path's budget is spent at the barrier and the log, not in the map, so the next engine's durable-load promise is registered against the raw+index arm, ~1.0M ops/s on this host.

Today's engine commits at 203,603 ops/s against the 1,191,125 floor -- 5.85x below, p=0.0022, mid-band of the registered 3-8x. The gap is per-point arena append + section work that a WAL-only design deletes rather than optimizes, and 5.85x is the number the rewrite is claiming to recover. Read with F39.1: the floor clears LMDB by 2.08x and today's engine sits 2.8x below LMDB, so the whole 0.348x deficit on EXT.9 lives between the engine and its own floor, none of it in the hardware.

Per-segment blocked Blooms keep 82.1% of the single-store read rate at sixteen segments -- 1.693x over the unfiltered fan (p=0.0022) but only 0.683x of the oracle, inside the 60-85% band registered in filter-plan.md. The mechanism is structural, not tunable: a fixed probe order queries ~8.5 filters per lookup before its first data probe, so per-segment filtering recreates the fan tax at a smaller constant and cannot reach the ceiling at this k.

Registered prediction P2 said a global key->segment map recovers 95% of perfect routing; it recovers 61.7% (765ns/read against the oracle's 472, p=0.0022) and loses to the per-segment blooms it was supposed to beat. The refutation clause named the cause in advance: a routing map's real cost is not its lookup arithmetic but its memory misses -- a std hash map at 1M entries pays ~290ns of SipHash and DRAM walk per query. The re-examination it demanded is f41: a routing structure has to answer in one cache miss or it is not a routing structure.

Min/max fences prune nothing when segment key-ranges overlap: fence16 within noise of the unfiltered fan (0.918x, p=0.0553, no difference). Round-robin dealing makes every segment's range cover every key and the fence admits every probe. Recorded so the design never assumes fences route without key-partitioned sealing; they are a compaction-policy benefit, not a general router.
